title: Enforce Accountability, Human Oversight, and Auditing
intro: Human oversight as a governance matter: HITL and HOTL accountability, and who holds the authority to intervene, override, sign off and stop. Then shadow AI detection and management, the governance artefacts that prove accountability, labelling AI interactions and synthetic content, and internal and external audits of compliance, bias, drift and outcomes.
objectives: Define accountability and enablers for HITL and HOTL oversight, and assign intervention, override, sign-off and stop authorities
Design escalation paths with an emergency stop, and record every exercise of authority
Detect shadow AI through network, SaaS, endpoint, finance and code sources, and manage it without driving it underground
Produce and maintain governance artefacts: model cards, system documentation, datasheets, assessments, decision logs and exception records
Apply AI interaction and synthetic content labelling duties, and choose marking techniques
Plan internal and external AI audits covering compliance, bias, drift, security, outcomes and governance

scenes.sub: Oversight models, and the authority to intervene, override and sign off
scenes.say: Human oversight is only as strong as the authority behind it. A reviewer who can’t say no, or an operator who doesn’t know they may pull the plug, provides no protection at all. | This video looks at oversight from a governance angle: who holds which authority, how it is exercised, and how it is recorded.

scenes.say: Oversight relies on four distinct authorities. | Intervention: the power to pause, adjust or redirect a running process, such as holding an agent’s queue of actions. | Override: the power to replace the AI’s output with a human decision, for example reversing a declined application. | Sign-off: formal approval at defined gates, such as going live, making a significant change, or accepting residual risk. | And stop: the power to halt the system entirely, immediately and safely. note.text: Stopping is never wrong when harm is imminent; investigate afterwards.

blocks.md:
### Oversight from a governance perspective
Module 1.3 described **human-in-the-loop (HITL)**, **human-on-the-loop (HOTL)** and automated operation as operational modes. Governance asks a different question: *who is accountable, who holds which authority, and how do we know they can and do exercise it?* The EU AI Act puts this into law for high-risk systems: deployers must assign human oversight to people with the necessary **competence, training and authority** (Article 26), and systems must allow overseers to override, reverse or interrupt them (Article 14).

| | HITL governance | HOTL governance |
|---|---|---|
| Accountability | The approver owns each decision they sign off | The supervisor owns timely intervention; the system owner owns the design of alerts and controls |
| Key enablers | Evidence presented with each recommendation; realistic workload; authority to refuse | Dashboards, meaningful alerts, tested stop and rollback controls, on-call cover |
| Metrics | Override and reject rates, review time per case, sampled quality of approvals | Time to detect and intervene, alert precision, frequency of interventions |
| Typical failure | Rubber-stamping through automation bias and volume | Alert fatigue; supervision assigned to someone without time or authority |

### The four authorities
- **Intervention authority:** the right to pause, throttle, reroute or adjust a running system or workflow (for example, holding an agent’s pending actions, or routing all cases to manual review).
- **Override authority:** the right to replace an AI output with a human decision in an individual case. Overrides should be easy, recorded with a reason, and analysed: patterns of overrides reveal model problems.
- **Sign-off authority:** formal approval at lifecycle gates: design approval, pre-deployment approval, approval of significant changes, and acceptance of residual risk. Sign-off must be by someone with authority proportionate to the risk tier.
- **Stop authority:** the right to halt a system entirely. It should be held by several people (operations, system owner, security), exercisable at any time, backed by a tested **kill switch** or circuit breaker (Module 5.7), and protected by a policy that good-faith stops are never penalised.

### Authority matrices and RACI
A **RACI** matrix records who is **Responsible** (does the work), **Accountable** (owns the outcome; one person), **Consulted** and **Informed** for each activity. For AI, extend it with explicit **decision rights** and **deputies**, so that authority is never unavailable at the moment it is needed. Typical rows: approving a use case, approving deployment, approving model changes, overriding decisions, invoking emergency stop, accepting residual risk, approving exceptions, and approving retirement.

### Escalation
Escalation paths should be documented, short, and tested:
1. **Front-line reviewers or operators** raise concerns through a defined channel.
2. The **system owner** investigates and can intervene or adjust.
3. Policy questions, significant risks and disputes go to the **AI governance committee**.
4. Residual risk beyond the committee’s authority goes to an **executive** or the board.

The **emergency path** bypasses the hierarchy: where harm is imminent (for example, an agent making unauthorised payments, or a model producing dangerous advice at scale), anyone with stop authority halts the system first. Speed matters more than permission in that moment, and the post-incident review examines the decision later.

### Records
Every use of authority should leave a record: approvals and sign-offs with their evidence, overrides with reasons, interventions and stops with timestamps and effects. These records are **governance artefacts** (Section 3) and core **audit evidence** (Section 4).

pairs: A claims handler reverses the model’s recommendation to deny a claim
The governance committee approves a tier-3 system for production
An operator pauses an agent’s outgoing emails while a pattern is investigated
The on-call engineer disables a chatbot that is giving dangerous advice

blocks.title: Authority must match accountability
blocks.md: Look for answers where the person exercising oversight has **competence, time, information and authority**. Distractors include oversight assigned to someone junior with no power to act, approval by the team that built the system, or a kill switch that requires a committee meeting to use.

blocks.title: The weekend agent
blocks.md: An agent processes supplier refunds 24 hours a day. On Saturday night, monitoring shows it issuing refunds at ten times the normal rate. The on-call engineer can see the problem but believes only the head of finance may stop the system, and she can’t be reached until Monday.

q.q: What governance failure does this MOST clearly reveal?
o: The model was not accurate enough, so the agent misread the situation and took harmful actions
Stop authority wasn’t assigned to available, trained people with a tested kill switch and protection
The monitoring threshold was too sensitive, so staff had learned to ignore alerts from the agent
The agent should have run only during office hours, when more people were available to supervise it
q.why: Monitoring worked, but nobody available believed they could act. Stop authority must be held by people on call, documented, practised and protected, so harm can be halted immediately and reviewed afterwards.

q.q: Under the EU AI Act, what must deployers of high-risk systems ensure about the people assigned to human oversight?
o: They are the system’s developers, who understand how it works
They have the necessary competence, training and authority
They review a sample of outputs at least once each year
They are external consultants, to guarantee independence
q.why: Article 26 requires deployers to assign oversight to natural persons with the competence, training and authority needed, and Article 14 requires systems to let them override or interrupt the system.

scenes.title: AI you didn’t approve
scenes.sub: Finding shadow AI, and bringing it into the light
scenes.say: In almost every organisation, people are using AI tools that nobody approved. Usually they are trying to do their jobs better, not to cause harm. | This video covers the forms shadow AI takes, why it matters, how to detect it, and why managing it works better than simply blocking it.

scenes.title: Forms of shadow AI

items.d: Personal accounts used with work data
New capabilities switched on by default
Browser add-ons that read every page
Scripts and agents calling models directly
Open-weight models downloaded and run on laptops
Teams building AI outside governance

scenes.say: Shadow AI takes many forms. | Public chatbots used through personal accounts, with work data pasted in. | New AI features inside already-approved SaaS products, sometimes switched on by default in an update. | Browser extensions and plug-ins that can read every page a user visits, including internal systems. | Personal API keys used in scripts and agents that call models directly. | Open-weight models downloaded and run locally on laptops. | And AI systems built by teams that simply never registered them with governance.

scenes.title: Why it matters

items.d: Confidential and personal data sent to unvetted providers
Consumer terms may allow retention and training
Unassessed transfers, AI Act duties, records rules
Decisions based on unchecked AI answers
No logs, no inventory, no incident response

scenes.say: Why does it matter? | Data leakage: confidential and personal data flows to providers nobody has assessed. | No contract protection: consumer terms may allow the provider to retain inputs and train on them. | Compliance blind spots: unassessed international transfers, unmet AI Act duties, and records that should have been kept. | Unvetted outputs: business decisions based on AI answers nobody checked. | And no visibility: no logs, no inventory entry, and no way to respond when something goes wrong.

scenes.title: Where to look
scenes.say: Detection needs several sources feeding one register, which is then triaged into the AI inventory. | Network, proxy and DNS logs, often through a secure web gateway or cloud access security broker, reveal traffic to AI services. | SaaS management tools and OAuth grants show which applications users have connected to corporate accounts, and which have new AI features. | Endpoint management reveals browser extensions and locally installed models. | Expense claims and procurement records reveal paid AI subscriptions. | And code and secret scanning reveals API keys and model calls in repositories. Surveys and amnesties fill the gaps.

scenes.title: Managing what you find
scenes.intro: Treat discoveries as demand signals, not just violations.

stages.label: Triage
stages.d: What data, which users, what risk?

stages.label: Decide
stages.d: Approve, replace with a sanctioned tool, or block.

stages.label: Monitor
stages.d: Watch for recurrence and new tools.

scenes.say: Managing shadow AI is a cycle. | Discover continuously, from several sources. | Triage each finding: what data is involved, who is using it, and how risky it is. | Decide: approve it through a fast-track route, replace it with a sanctioned alternative, or block it where the risk is unacceptable. | Enable people with approved tools, clear guidance and training, so they don’t need workarounds. | And monitor for recurrence and new tools. Treat every discovery as a signal of unmet demand, not just a violation.

items.d: Personal phones, home networks, new tools
People use AI because it helps them
Enterprise tools with data protection
DLP and classification, wherever data flows

scenes.say: Blanket blocking usually fails. | People find workarounds: personal phones, home networks, and tools the blocklist hasn’t caught yet, which leaves you with less visibility, not more. | The demand is real, because AI genuinely helps people with their work. | The better approach is a sanctioned path: enterprise tools with contractual data protection, approved quickly. | And protect the data itself, with classification and data loss prevention that apply wherever data flows, including into AI tools.

blocks.md:
### What counts as shadow AI
**Shadow AI** is the use of AI tools, models or features without the organisation’s knowledge, approval or governance. It is a special case of shadow IT, with extra risks because AI tools ingest whatever users give them and produce outputs people may rely on. Common forms:
- personal accounts on public chatbots and image generators used for work;
- **embedded AI** features added to approved SaaS products, sometimes enabled by default;
- browser extensions, meeting bots and plug-ins with broad access to pages, mailboxes or calendars;
- personal or team API keys used in scripts, spreadsheets, low-code tools and agents;
- open-weight models run locally or on unmanaged cloud accounts;
- models and agents built by business teams without registration or assessment.

### Risks
| Risk | Example |
|---|---|
| Data leakage | Source code, customer records or board papers pasted into a consumer chatbot whose terms permit retention and training |
| Contractual and legal gaps | No data processing agreement, unknown sub-processors, unassessed international transfers |
| Regulatory exposure | An unregistered high-risk use (for example, screening job applicants) with none of the required controls |
| Security | Extensions or agents with broad tokens; malicious tools posing as AI helpers; leaked API keys |
| Quality and liability | Decisions or customer communications based on unverified AI output |
| Loss of visibility | No inventory entry, no logs, no incident detection or response |

### Detection techniques
- **Network and web gateway telemetry** (secure web gateways, CASB/SSE, DNS logs, firewall logs) identifies traffic to known AI services and categorises it.
- **SaaS discovery and OAuth/app-consent reviews** show third-party apps connected to corporate identities and the scopes granted, plus vendor release notes announcing new AI features.
- **Endpoint management** inventories browser extensions, installed applications and local model runtimes.
- **Data loss prevention** on endpoints and in the browser flags sensitive data being pasted or uploaded into AI tools.
- **Finance and procurement** reviews reveal subscriptions bought on cards or expensed.
- **Code and secret scanning** finds API keys and calls to model endpoints in repositories and pipelines.
- **People-based methods**: surveys, AI champions, and **amnesty** periods where teams can register tools without penalty.

### Managing shadow AI
1. **Triage** each discovery by data sensitivity, user population and purpose.
2. **Decide**: approve via a **fast-track** route for low-risk tools; **replace** with a sanctioned alternative; or **block** where risk is unacceptable (for example, tools whose terms allow training on confidential inputs).
3. **Enable**: publish an approved-tools list, provide enterprise versions with contractual protections, and train staff on the acceptable use policy.
4. **Protect data directly**: classification labels and DLP policies that apply in browsers and AI tools, and identity-based controls (single sign-on, conditional access) for sanctioned tools.
5. **Monitor and measure**: track the number of unsanctioned tools, sensitive-data events, time to approve requests, and adoption of sanctioned alternatives.

The most effective programmes treat shadow AI as **demand intelligence**: each unsanctioned tool shows a need that governance hasn’t met yet.

blocks.title: Shadow AI responses
items: Marketing image generator
Discovered through expense claims. **Data:** brand assets and campaign briefs, low sensitivity. **Decision:** fast-track approval of an enterprise licence with IP indemnity; add to the approved list.
Code assistant extension

Discovered by endpoint inventory. **Data:** proprietary source code sent to an unvetted provider. **Decision:** remove the extension; provide an approved code assistant with no-training terms and code-licence filters.
Meeting transcription bot

Discovered when it joined a board meeting. **Data:** highly confidential discussions. **Decision:** block unmanaged meeting bots tenant-wide; offer the platform’s approved transcription feature with retention controls.
Team-built triage agent

Discovered through secret scanning (an API key in a repository). **Data:** customer emails. **Decision:** rotate the key, register the agent in the inventory, tier it, and complete an assessment before it can continue.

blocks.title: The balanced answer
blocks.md: For shadow AI questions, the best answer usually **combines discovery with enablement**: detect and triage, provide sanctioned alternatives, update the acceptable use policy and training, and protect sensitive data with DLP. Answers that only **ban** AI, or only **ignore** it, are rarely correct.

q.q: Network logs show hundreds of employees using a consumer AI chatbot, some pasting customer data. What is the BEST first response?
o: Block all AI domains permanently, and discipline the employees who pasted customer data into the tool
Triage the risk, offer an approved enterprise alternative, communicate the policy, and apply DLP rules
Ask the chatbot provider to delete the organisation’s data, and note the incident in the risk register
Monitor usage for another quarter to measure how widespread the practice is before deciding what to do
q.why: Blanket blocking drives use underground and doesn’t meet the demand. A sanctioned alternative, clear policy and data protection reduce risk while keeping visibility.

scenes.title: The paper trail, and the label
scenes.sub: Governance artefacts, and telling people when AI is involved
scenes.say: Accountability needs evidence. If it isn’t written down, it didn’t happen, at least as far as an auditor or regulator is concerned. And people affected by AI deserve to know when it is involved. | This video covers the core governance artefacts, and how AI interactions and synthetic content should be labelled.

scenes.title: Core governance artefacts

items.d: Purpose, training data, performance by group, limits
The whole system: components, safeguards, oversight
Provenance, composition, collection, permitted uses
Risk, impact, DPIA and test reports
Who decided what, when, on what evidence
Waived requirements, compensating controls, expiry

scenes.say: Six artefacts form the core of an AI paper trail. | A model card describes a model’s purpose, training data, performance across groups and known limitations. | System documentation describes the whole system around the model: components, safeguards and oversight. | A datasheet for a dataset records its provenance, composition, collection method and permitted uses. | Assessments include risk and impact assessments, DPIAs and test reports. | Decision logs record who decided what, when, and on what evidence, from approvals to individual overrides. | And exception records capture any policy requirement that was waived, with compensating controls and an expiry date.

scenes.title: Decision logs and exception records
rows: Significant decisions about the system
A departure from policy or a standard
Decision, maker, date, evidence, rationale
Requirement waived, reason, controls, approver, expiry
Sampled by audit; used in investigations
Before expiry; tracked in a register
scenes.say: Two artefacts are often confused. | A decision log records significant decisions about the system. An exception record documents a departure from policy or a standard. | A decision log entry captures the decision, who made it, when, the evidence considered and the rationale. An exception record captures which requirement was waived, why, the compensating controls, who approved it and when it expires. | Decision logs are sampled by auditors and used in investigations. Exceptions are tracked in a register and reviewed before they expire, so temporary exceptions don’t quietly become permanent.

scenes.title: When people must be told (EU AI Act Article 50)

items.d: Disclose AI interaction unless it is obvious
Providers mark outputs in machine-readable form
Deployers disclose manipulated or generated likenesses
Disclose AI text unless a human took editorial responsibility
Inform the people exposed to it

scenes.say: The EU AI Act’s transparency rules, which have applied since August twenty twenty-six, set out when people must be told. | Providers must design systems that interact with people so they know they are talking to AI, unless that is obvious. | Providers of generative systems must mark outputs in a machine-readable, detectable way. | Deployers must disclose deepfakes: images, audio or video that resemble real people, places or events. | Deployers publishing AI-generated text on matters of public interest must disclose it, unless a person reviewed it and took editorial responsibility. | And people exposed to emotion recognition or biometric categorisation must be informed.

scenes.title: Ways to mark synthetic content

items.d: Clear to people; easily cropped or removed
Embedded signals; need a detector; can be degraded
Signed history such as C2PA; often stripped
No cooperation needed; error-prone

scenes.say: There are four main ways to mark synthetic content, and none is perfect on its own. | Visible labels are clear to people, but easily cropped or removed. | Invisible watermarks embed a signal in the content itself. They need a detector, and editing or compression can degrade them. | Provenance metadata, such as C2PA content credentials, records a signed history of how content was made and edited, but many platforms strip metadata. | And detection classifiers try to spot synthetic content without any cooperation from its creator, but they make errors in both directions. So combine methods: label for people, and mark for machines.

items: Model cards, system docs, datasheets, assessments, decision logs, exceptions
Exceptions need compensating controls and an expiry date
Disclose AI interaction, deepfakes and public-interest text
Combine visible labels, watermarks and provenance
scenes.say: To recap. | The core artefacts are model cards, system documentation, datasheets, assessments, decision logs and exception records. | Every exception needs compensating controls, an approver and an expiry date. | Tell people when they are interacting with AI, and disclose deepfakes and AI-generated public-interest text. | And mark synthetic content in layers: visible labels for people, watermarks and provenance metadata for machines.

blocks.md:
### Governance artefacts
Artefacts are how an organisation **demonstrates** accountability: to auditors, regulators, customers, courts and its own staff. ISO/IEC 42001 requires documented information; the EU AI Act requires technical documentation, logs and records for high-risk systems; and every audit starts by asking for evidence.

| Artefact | Purpose | Typical contents |
|---|---|---|
| **Model card** | Transparency about a model | Intended use and out-of-scope uses, training data overview, evaluation results including performance across groups, limitations, ethical considerations |
| **System card / AI system documentation** | Transparency about the deployed system | Architecture, components and third parties, safeguards and guardrails, human oversight design, monitoring, known risks |
| **Datasheet for datasets** | Accountability for data | Motivation, composition, collection process, preprocessing, consent and licensing, recommended and prohibited uses, maintenance |
| **Risk and impact assessments** | Evidence of due diligence | Risk register entries, impact assessments, DPIAs, FRIAs, tier decisions |
| **Test and evaluation reports** | Evidence of fitness | Accuracy, robustness, bias, security and red-team results, with versions tested |
| **Decision logs** | Traceability of decisions | Design choices, approvals and sign-offs, risk acceptances, model change approvals, and records of overrides and interventions |
| **Exception records** | Control of deviations | Requirement waived, justification, compensating controls, risk owner, approver, **expiry date**, review |
| **Operational logs** | Traceability of system behaviour | Inputs, outputs, model versions, tool calls and human actions, retained according to policy (Domain 5) |

Good artefacts are **versioned** (tied to specific model and system versions), **owned** (someone keeps them current), **accessible** to those who need them, and **retained** according to legal and policy requirements. Model cards and datasheets also make excellent procurement requests (Module 2.5).

### AI interaction labelling
People have a reasonable interest, and increasingly a legal right, to know when AI is involved. Under **Article 50 of the EU AI Act** (applying from 2 August 2026):
- **Providers** must ensure systems intended to interact directly with people inform them they are interacting with AI, unless obvious from the context.
- **Providers** of systems generating synthetic audio, images, video or text must ensure outputs are **marked in a machine-readable format and detectable** as artificially generated or manipulated. Systems already on the market before 2 August 2026 had until 2 December 2026 to comply with this marking duty.
- **Deployers** of emotion recognition or biometric categorisation must inform the people exposed.
- **Deployers** must disclose **deepfakes**, with a lighter touch for evidently artistic, creative, satirical or fictional works.
- **Deployers** publishing AI-generated or manipulated **text on matters of public interest** must disclose it, unless it underwent human review and a person holds editorial responsibility.

A voluntary EU **Code of Practice on the transparency of AI-generated content**, with common labelling icons, and Commission guidelines published in July 2026, support implementation. Other jurisdictions have their own rules; China, for example, introduced mandatory labelling of AI-generated content in 2025.

### Marking techniques
| Technique | Strengths | Weaknesses |
|---|---|---|
| **Visible labels and icons** | Understandable by people; simple | Removable by cropping or editing; can be ignored |
| **Invisible watermarks** | Survive some transformations; machine-detectable | Need the right detector; can be degraded or removed by determined actors; robustness varies, especially for text |
| **Provenance metadata (C2PA content credentials)** | Cryptographically signed history of creation and edits; supports trust in authentic content too | Often stripped by platforms and screenshots; relies on adoption |
| **Detection classifiers** | Work without the creator’s cooperation | False positives and negatives; easily fooled; shouldn’t be the sole basis for accusations |

The practical answer is **layered**: label clearly for humans at the point of interaction, embed machine-readable marks and provenance where possible, log what was generated, and never rely on detection alone for consequential decisions (such as accusing a student or employee of using AI). Organisations should also protect themselves against **impersonation**: deepfake voices and videos of executives are used in fraud, so payment and access requests need out-of-band verification regardless of how convincing the request appears.

blocks.title: Artefact vocabulary
cards: A document describing a model’s intended use, data, performance across groups and limitations.
A document recording a dataset’s motivation, composition, collection, licensing and appropriate uses.
A record of significant decisions: what, who, when, evidence and rationale.
A documented, approved and time-limited departure from a policy or standard, with compensating controls.
An open standard for signed provenance metadata describing how content was created and edited.
AI-generated or manipulated image, audio or video that resembles real people, objects, places or events.

blocks.title: The permanent exception
blocks.md: Two years ago, a team received an exception allowing its customer-facing chatbot to launch without bias testing “for three months” while a testing tool was procured. Nobody tracked the expiry. The chatbot now handles 40% of customer contacts, and the exception has never been reviewed.

q.q: Which control MOST directly prevents this situation?
o: A policy banning all exceptions to AI security requirements, with no further approvals permitted
An exception register with owners, compensating controls, expiry dates and review before expiry
A reminder in the team’s calendar asking the project lead to remember the deadline for the fix
Annual staff training on the exception process, refreshed whenever the AI policy is updated
q.why: Exceptions are legitimate when controlled. A register with owners and expiry-driven review stops temporary exceptions becoming permanent, unmanaged risk. Banning exceptions would push deviations underground.

q.q: A company deploys a customer-service chatbot in the EU. Under Article 50 of the AI Act, what must happen?
o: Nothing, because chatbots are classed as minimal risk and have no specific obligations
People must be told they are interacting with AI, unless that is obvious from the context
The chatbot must be registered in the EU database as a high-risk system before launch
Every response must be approved by a trained human before it is sent to the customer
q.why: Article 50 requires systems that interact directly with people to disclose that they are AI unless it is obvious. It is a transparency duty, not a high-risk classification.

scenes.sub: Internal and external audits for compliance, bias, drift and business outcomes
scenes.say: Policies, assessments and controls all claim that AI is under control. Audits test whether those claims are true. | This video covers internal and external AI audits, what they examine, how they work, and what makes AI harder to audit than ordinary systems.

scenes.title: Internal and external audits

Independent third parties, certification bodies, notified bodies
Assurance to the board; drive improvement
Certification, legal requirements, public trust
ISO/IEC 42001 internal audit; AI control reviews
42001 certification; bias audits of hiring tools; AI Act conformity assessment
scenes.say: Audits come in two kinds. | Internal audits are performed by the organisation’s internal audit function, which must be independent of the teams it audits. External audits are performed by independent third parties, such as certification bodies, specialist auditors or, for some high-risk AI products, notified bodies. | Internal audit gives the board assurance and drives improvement. External audit supports certification, legal requirements and public trust. | Examples include the internal audits ISO forty-two thousand and one requires, certification audits against it, independent bias audits of hiring tools required in some jurisdictions, and conformity assessments under the AI Act.

scenes.title: What AI audits examine

items.d: Laws, policies, contracts, documentation
Outcomes and error rates across groups
Still valid? Is monitoring working?
Controls, testing results, incident handling
Benefits delivered, costs, unintended effects
Inventory complete; approvals actually followed

scenes.say: AI audits can examine six areas. | Compliance with laws, policies, contracts and documentation requirements. | Bias and fairness, by testing outcomes and error rates across groups. | Drift and performance: is the system still valid, and is monitoring actually catching problems? | Security: whether controls work, what testing found, and how incidents were handled. | Business outcomes: whether the system delivers the benefits that justified it, at acceptable cost, without unintended effects. | And the governance process itself: is the inventory complete, and were approvals, assessments and reviews actually followed?

scenes.title: How an AI audit runs
scenes.say: An audit follows a familiar process, with AI-specific techniques. Planning sets the scope based on risk, usually focusing on high-tier systems and recent changes. | Evidence gathering collects artefacts, logs and monitoring data, and interviews owners and reviewers. | Testing checks that controls work, by sampling decisions, re-running evaluations, testing for bias and verifying that monitoring alerts fire. | The report rates each finding by severity and assigns an owner and a deadline. | Owners remediate, and the auditor follows up to verify the fix actually works.

scenes.title: Why AI is harder to audit

items.d: Vendor models are black boxes: secure audit rights by contract
Re-run tests many times and assess rates
Testing needs data; protect privacy while sampling
Systems drift; move towards continuous auditing
AI audits need technical and ethical expertise

scenes.say: AI raises particular audit challenges. | Opacity: vendor models are black boxes, so audit rights and evidence must be secured in the contract. | Non-determinism: the same test can pass and fail, so tests are run many times and results assessed as rates. | Data access: testing for bias or leakage needs data, which must be handled with privacy safeguards. | A moving target: systems drift between audits, which is pushing organisations towards continuous auditing using monitoring data. | And skills: auditors need enough technical and ethical expertise to challenge AI teams effectively.

blocks.md:
### Internal and external audits
| | Internal audit | External audit |
|---|---|---|
| Performed by | The organisation’s internal audit function (the third line), independent of the audited teams | Independent third parties: certification bodies, specialist assurance firms, regulators’ appointees, notified bodies |
| Reports to | The board or audit committee | The organisation, and sometimes regulators or the public |
| Purpose | Independent assurance that governance, risk management and controls work; improvement | Certification (for example ISO/IEC 42001), legally required audits, conformity assessment, customer assurance |
| Examples | ISO/IEC 42001 clause 9.2 internal audits; reviews of AI controls and model risk | ISO/IEC 42001 certification audits (by bodies meeting ISO/IEC 42006); bias audits of automated employment decision tools in New York City; conformity assessment of certain high-risk AI systems under the EU AI Act |

Independence is essential: the team that built or operates a system can test it (first line), and risk or compliance teams can review it (second line), but neither is an **audit**.

### Audit scopes for AI
- **Compliance:** legal requirements (AI Act roles and duties, GDPR, sector rules), internal policies and standards, contractual commitments, and documentation completeness.
- **Bias and fairness:** recomputing fairness metrics on representative samples, reviewing data and features for proxies, and checking that monitoring tracks group outcomes. NYC Local Law 144, for example, requires annual independent bias audits of automated employment decision tools, with impact ratios published.
- **Drift and performance:** comparing current performance with validated baselines, checking drift thresholds, and verifying that alerts reach owners and lead to action.
- **Security:** reviewing threat models, test and red-team results, vulnerability management, access controls for models and data, and AI incident handling.
- **Business outcomes:** whether the system delivers the benefits in its business case, at acceptable cost, without harmful side effects (for example, rising complaint rates).
- **Governance process:** inventory completeness (reconciled against discovery data), tiering accuracy, assessments completed before deployment, sign-offs by the right authority, exception management, and human oversight in practice (for example, override rates).

### Evidence
Typical evidence includes the AI inventory and AIBOMs; tier decisions; risk and impact assessments; model cards and system documentation; test, evaluation and red-team reports; decision logs and exception registers; monitoring dashboards and alert histories; operational logs of prompts, outputs, tool calls and human interventions (with privacy safeguards); change records; incident records; and training records for people with oversight roles.

### Audit techniques for AI
- **Sampling and re-performance:** select decisions and trace them through logs, including any human review, and check the outcome against policy.
- **Independent re-testing:** re-run evaluation suites, fairness metrics and adversarial tests, ideally with the auditor’s own test data.
- **Control testing:** verify that kill switches, overrides and alerts actually work.
- **Reconciliation:** compare the inventory with discovery data to find unregistered AI.
- **Interviews and walkthroughs:** confirm that people with oversight roles understand and exercise their authority.

### Challenges and responses
| Challenge | Response |
|---|---|
| Opaque vendor models | Contractual audit rights, independent assurance reports, model and system cards, and black-box testing of outputs |
| Non-determinism | Repeat tests; report rates and confidence intervals; pin versions during testing |
| Privacy of test data | Minimise, pseudonymise, use secure environments, and involve the DPO |
| Drift between audits | **Continuous auditing** using monitoring data and automated control checks, supplemented by periodic deep reviews |
| Auditor competence | Training, specialist co-sourcing and multidisciplinary audit teams |

blocks.title: Which audit scope?
pairs: Recalculating impact ratios on last quarter’s hiring decisions
Checking that every production model appears in the inventory
Verifying that drift alerts reached the owner and were acted on
Comparing promised cost savings with actual results
Reviewing red-team findings and their remediation

blocks.title: Independence and evidence
blocks.md: An audit must be **independent** of the activity audited, and conclusions must rest on **evidence**, not assurances. If an option has the development team “audit” its own model, or relies on a vendor’s marketing claims, it is not the best answer. Look for independent testing, sampled evidence, and tracked remediation.

q.q: Which of these provides the MOST independent assurance that an AI hiring tool is free of unlawful bias?
o: The data science team’s own fairness report, which uses the same data the tool was trained on
The vendor’s signed statement that the tool is unbiased, backed by its published model card
An independent audit that recomputes outcome metrics on representative data and checks for proxies
A survey of recruiters who use the tool every day and can report whether outcomes seem fair
q.why: Independent re-testing on representative data, including proxy analysis, gives the strongest assurance. Self-assessment and vendor claims lack independence, and user surveys don’t measure outcomes.

quiz.q: What MOST distinguishes human-on-the-loop from human-in-the-loop oversight?
o: HOTL means no human is involved at all; HITL means a human reviews a random sample of the decisions made afterwards
In HOTL the system acts while a person supervises and can intervene; in HITL a person approves each decision
HOTL is used only for chatbots, while HITL is used for every other type of high-risk AI system
HITL requires the system to run offline in batches, while HOTL lets it run in real time
quiz.why: The difference is when the human acts: before each decision (HITL) or during operation with the ability to intervene (HOTL).

quiz.q: A claims handler replaces a model’s “deny” recommendation with an approval. Which authority is being exercised?
o: Sign-off
Override
Stop
Audit
quiz.why: Override authority replaces an AI output with a human decision in an individual case. Overrides should be recorded with a reason and analysed for patterns.

quiz.q: Which practice BEST ensures an emergency stop can be used when needed?
o: Requiring a committee vote before any system is stopped, to prevent unnecessary disruption
Giving stop authority to several available, trained people, with a tested kill switch and protection
Keeping the kill switch procedure confidential, so attackers can’t learn how to trigger it
Allowing only the CEO to stop systems, so that stop decisions are always taken at the top
quiz.why: Stops must be fast. Available holders, practised controls and a no-blame policy make the authority real.

quiz.q: Which is an example of shadow AI?
o: An enterprise chatbot approved through governance and listed in the inventory
An employee using a personal public chatbot account to summarise confidential reports
A model listed in the AI inventory that has not been reassessed for two years
A vendor tool with a signed data processing agreement that staff use for translation
quiz.why: Shadow AI is AI used without the organisation’s knowledge, approval or governance, often with consumer terms that offer no data protection.

quiz.q: Which source is MOST useful for discovering third-party AI apps that users have connected to corporate accounts?
o: Building access logs showing which staff were on site
OAuth and app-consent records from the identity platform and SaaS discovery tools
Printer and scanner logs showing documents that were digitised
An annual staff survey asking which AI tools and browser extensions people use at work
quiz.why: App-consent records show which third-party applications have been granted access to corporate identities and data, and with what scopes.

quiz.q: What must an exception record include to keep exceptions under control?
o: Only the requester’s name and the date the exception was requested
The requirement waived, justification, compensating controls, approver and expiry date
The model’s source code and configuration at the time the exception was first raised by the team
A copy of the policy being waived, signed by everyone affected by the exception
quiz.why: Without compensating controls and expiry-driven review, temporary exceptions become permanent unmanaged risk.

quiz.q: Which document describes a model’s intended use, training data, performance across groups and limitations?
o: A datasheet for datasets
A model card
An SBOM
A risk acceptance
quiz.why: Model cards provide transparency about a specific model. Datasheets describe datasets; system documentation describes the whole deployed system.

quiz.q: Under the EU AI Act, who must disclose that an image is a deepfake?
o: Nobody, provided the image is clearly artistic or satirical
The deployer who uses the system to generate or manipulate the content
Only the cloud provider that hosts the image generation service
Only the person depicted, who must label every published image of themselves
quiz.why: Article 50 places the deepfake disclosure duty on deployers; providers must ensure generated content is machine-readably marked.

quiz.q: Which marking technique records a signed history of how content was created and edited?
o: Visible captions added to the image
Provenance metadata such as C2PA content credentials
Detection classifiers run by social media platforms on upload
Lossy compression that leaves editing artefacts
quiz.why: C2PA content credentials attach cryptographically signed provenance. Their weakness is that platforms often strip metadata.

quiz.q: Why is independence essential to an AI audit?
o: It makes audits faster, because independent auditors don’t need to learn the system
Assurance is only credible when the auditor is independent of those who built and run the system
Independent auditors can rely on their own judgement, so they need less evidence from the team
It removes the need for remediation, because independent findings are advisory rather than binding
quiz.why: Self-assessment is useful but isn’t assurance. Independence, plus evidence, makes audit conclusions trustworthy.

quiz.q: Which technique BEST addresses the non-determinism of generative AI during an audit?
o: Running each test once on the latest model version to save time
Repeating tests many times with pinned versions and assessing rates
Accepting the vendor’s published test results for each model version
Setting temperature to zero, which makes generative outputs fully repeatable
quiz.why: Because outputs vary, single runs prove little, and even temperature 0 doesn’t guarantee identical outputs. Repeated runs against pinned versions give rates that can be compared with thresholds.

exam.q: A bank assigns HOTL supervision of an automated fraud-blocking model to one analyst, who also handles 150 customer calls a day. Blocked-account complaints rise for weeks before anyone acts. What is the MOST significant governance flaw?
o: The model’s blocking threshold was set too high, so too many genuine customers were blocked
Oversight was assigned without the time, alerting and authority needed to supervise effectively
Customers complained too much, which made genuine fraud alerts harder for the analyst to spot
The model should have been human-in-the-loop for every decision, however small the amount involved
exam.why: HOTL needs real-time visibility, meaningful alerts and people with capacity and authority to intervene. Nominal oversight by an overloaded analyst provides no protection.

exam.q: Who should normally hold sign-off authority for deploying a tier-3 (high-risk) AI system to production?
o: The developer who built it, who best understands its design and limitations
The governance committee or a designated senior owner, after required assessments and tests
The business users of the system, who will be accountable for its day-to-day outcomes and benefits
The cloud provider hosting the model, which is responsible for its production environment
exam.why: Sign-off authority must match the risk tier and be independent of the builders, with evidence that prerequisites are met.

exam.q: Secret scanning finds an API key for an external model in a sales team’s repository. The key is used by an unregistered agent that reads customer emails. What should happen FIRST?
o: Delete the repository and the agent’s code, then investigate who created them
Rotate the exposed key, then register, tier and assess the agent before it continues
Leave the agent running, since sales depends on it, and add it to next quarter’s review
Move the key to a private repository and ask the sales team to register the agent soon
exam.why: An exposed credential must be rotated immediately. The agent then needs to come under governance, with an inventory entry, tier and assessment, because it processes customer data.

exam.q: An auditor asks why a high-risk model was deployed without the required adversarial test. The team says the CTO verbally agreed. What does this reveal?
o: Nothing significant; verbal approval from a senior executive is sufficient for a one-off deviation
A missing exception record: deviations need justification, compensating controls, an approver and expiry
The auditor lacks the authority to question decisions approved by members of the executive leadership team
Adversarial testing is optional for high-risk models, so long as the CTO agrees the risk is low
exam.why: Undocumented deviations can’t be verified, reviewed or closed. Exception records make deviations visible, controlled and time-bound.

exam.q: A company uses AI to generate a realistic video of its CEO for a marketing campaign shown in the EU. What is required?
o: No disclosure, because the CEO consented to the use of their likeness in the campaign
Disclosure that the content is AI-generated or manipulated, plus machine-readable marking
Registration of the video in the EU database as the output of a high-risk AI system
Prior approval of the video from the data protection authority in each EU country
exam.why: Content resembling real people is a deepfake under Article 50. Deployers must disclose it, and generative systems must mark outputs. Consent doesn’t remove the transparency duty.

exam.q: An organisation’s annual AI audit keeps finding that drift had gone unnoticed for months. Which change BEST addresses this?
o: Audit every two years instead, with a larger sample of systems examined in much more depth on each occasion
Introduce continuous auditing using monitoring data and automated control checks, plus periodic reviews
Remove drift from the audit scope, since drift is a model quality issue rather than a control failure
Rely on vendor assurances about drift monitoring, since vendors have the best view of their models
exam.why: AI systems change between periodic audits. Continuous auditing detects control failures, such as missed drift alerts, much sooner.
